Yes, China can come to the rescue. 

Rumor is that China will increase product export quota in September. Let’s see. 

Article:

There’s one good reason oil prices have never roared quite as loudly as they could have during the Strait of Hormuz crisis: China. The People’s Republic slashed its imports of crude oil and drew from its huge stockpiles. Now, though, it’s diesel that’s in short supply, sending shockwaves through the economies of the US and Europe. Could China ride to the rescue again?

In theory, yes it could. The reason diesel is in short supply globally is because facilities that are available to refine crude oil into the preferred fuel for trucks, buses and trains are already running at full tilt. Many Russian refineries, formerly outsized producers of diesel, have been taken offline owing to attacks by Ukraine.

China, though, has ample spare capacity. Even before the US began its war with Iran, China had more refineries than it needed to supply its own domestic needs of oil-derived products. Its cuts to crude imports and product exports have left many plants half idle; in aggregate the 13mn barrels a day they are producing is 2.3mn barrels fewer than last February, WoodMackenzie estimates.

FT:

Long queues have formed at petrol stations around Tehran as the US blockade triggers fuel shortages and spreads alarm among motorists in a sign of the war’s growing strain on the Iranian economy.

The rush comes as Donald Trump’s administration outlined a new campaign of what it called “economic warfare” against Tehran, which the Energy Optimisation Organisation — an Iranian state body tasked with managing fuel resources — warned is facing a “critical” shortfall of petrol.

One petrol station attendant in the capital reported that people were rushing to fill up “even before their tanks are empty because they worry that the war might start over again or that prices will rise”. A limit of 20 litres per car meant that motorists had to keep returning, said the attendant, who did not want to be named.

tweets.text:
There are some many incorrect assumptions in that statement.

- Start with the mechanics. Yields do not rise because buyers vanish. Every bond that gets sold is bought by someone — the Treasury market clears every single day. Yields rise when the price buyers and sellers agree on falls, which happens when buyers demand more compensation to hold the paper, not when they walk away. And they haven't walked away. 
- The August 30-year auction drew 2.39 times more bids than there were bonds to sell — right in line with its five-year average of 2.37. That is a market pricing in heavy supply and a rising term premium, not a buyer's strike. 
- What's actually happening is more nuanced: the Fed is no longer buying, foreign official demand has softened at the margin, and the issuance calendar is enormous. So price-sensitive buyers want a better price. That is how markets are supposed to work. Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget
- Next, inflation. The idea that "so much money" has made inflation permanent ignores that it is currently decelerating. July CPI came in at 3.4%, down from 3.5%, with core at 2.5% — the lowest core reading in five months. 
-The uptick earlier this year was an energy shock tied to the conflict that erupted at the end of February, and that impulse is fading, not compounding. Running above the Fed's 2% target for a stretch is a cyclical overshoot. It is not the same thing as inflation being structurally embedded. CNBC + 2
- Finally, long bonds. Far from obsolete, they now yield roughly 5.27% on the 30-year versus the 2–3% they paid a decade ago. Higher yields make long duration more useful for income, not less. Pensions, insurers, and foreign central banks still need long-dated assets to match long-dated liabilities. That demand does not disappear. CNBC
- Your comment actually argues against itself. If yields are now above 5%, that is precisely the setup that historically pulls buyers back into long bonds. Such is the nature of markets: the cure for high yields is high yields.
